assessment: The ten buys redundancy where the audit measures the deck thinnest: a third lose-half for the two-card kill (the audit's own thinnest engine component, 2 cards, 9.4% assembled), two more sacrifice outlets behind a lone Viscera Seer, and the aristocrats ignition that turns a Grave Pact edict into drain. Per strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors, 'consistency has two purchases: redundancy (more cards doing the job) or tutoring (cards that fetch it)' — this list buys the first. The 34-card bench prunes hard before ranking even starts: two entries duplicate cards already in the 99, one sits outside Edgar's colour identity, and the obsolescence index says two more are strictly worse than cards already sleeved (Vampire Nocturnus behind Bloodline Keeper, Markov Purifier behind Preacher of the Schism). Three pool cards then beat what was left of the tail, and each entry below names the bench card it displaced. No pick in the ten carries an obsolescence claim: the index's fifteen straight upgrades over this deck are almost all out-of-tribe, and out-of-tribe in an eminence deck means no free token on cast.

Infinite lifegain triggers, infinite lifeloss, infinite lifegain

ten.closes: engine: The two-piece infinite assembled (a lose-half + a gain-half) — the audit's thinnest component, two cards, 13.7% in an opener
ten.why: The lose-half side of the kill is two cards deep — Vito and Sanguine Bond — and 'whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life' is a third that pairs with both gain-halves already sleeved; unlike Vito it drains every opponent, so a table of three takes 3 per trigger instead of 1.
ten.unlocks: Two more two-card pairings off the same board, taking the matrix from four to six; as a Vampire Cleric it also banks an eminence token on cast, so it arrives with a body attached.

ten.why: Viscera Seer is the deck's only free sacrifice outlet, and Grave Pact, Cruel Celebrant and every eminence token behind it stop working the turn it eats a removal spell; a second one-mana outlet whose activation also puts a +1/+1 counter on every Vampire keeps the edict engine live.
ten.when: Sleeve it as soon as a pod starts answering the Seer on sight — outlet redundancy is the purchase, not the counters.

ten.why: Cruel Celebrant only sees your own deaths; Blood Artist sees every creature that dies, so one Viscera Seer sacrifice under Grave Pact is four triggers — your token plus the three creatures the table is forced to sacrifice — draining 4 and gaining you 4 on a two-mana Vampire body.
ten.unlocks: That 4 life gained is the ignition the loop wants: with a lose-half and a gain-half both on the battlefield, any death becomes the trigger that starts the pairing. It is the best-ranked card anywhere in this analysis at EDHREC 138, and it beat Vampire Nighthawk for the two-to-three-mana Vampire slot — the Nighthawk is a body, this is an engine.

ten.why: Ramp measures 7 copies against a 10–12 target with no probe note under it, and this is the one bench card that answers it without a land: tap, sacrifice a spare eminence token, add {B}{B}{B} for Vampire, Cleric and Demon spells — a Grave Pact edict and a turn-four five-drop out of one activation.
ten.when: Sleeve it when opening hands keep stalling a turn behind the curve; it doubles as the third sacrifice outlet if pod speed makes the mana burst matter more than tribe-wide counters.

ten.why: Stack 002 settled that one {B}{B} Vampire cast makes four tokens through Anointed Procession and Mondrak; the Bats charge for tokens on the way in and again on the way out, so the same board that already feeds Purphoros and Viscera Seer starts draining on both halves of the transaction.
ten.unlocks: A non-combat clock off the token engine rather than the drain engine — it beat Blade of the Bloodchief for the slot, because the Blade needs a carrier and a combat step while the Bats need only the tokens the commander already makes from the command zone. Whether four simultaneous tokens are four triggers or one is the same entry-counting question stack 008 answered for Purphoros, and it is not settled for this card.

ten.why: A two-mana lifelink flier that becomes prepared in any second main phase you gained 2 or more life — routine on a board of lifelink Vampires — and a prepared Silvertongue lets you cast a copy of Sign in Blood for {B}{B}: draw two, lose two, every turn the tribe connects.
ten.when: Sleeve it when hands run empty by turn six or seven. Note the card-advantage axis reads 3 against a target of 10 but carries a probe note naming nine uncounted cards, so this is picked on what the card does, not on the axis reading.

ten.why: She counts every creature that dies, not just yours, so a Grave Pact edict feeds her three counters at a time — and she dies into that many 1/1 lifelink Vampire tokens, which the same Procession-and-Mondrak doubling stack 002 verified turns into four times as many bodies.
ten.when: Sleeve her for pods that sweep: she is the wrath-math payoff, the card that makes the table's answer to a wide board the worst turn of their game.

ten.why: Three opponents deploying artifacts and creatures means this taxes every one of their turns: tap the permanent or hand you a 1/1 lifelink Vampire, and those tokens are Vampires — Legion Lieutenant, Stromkirk Captain, Captivating Vampire and Shared Animosity all read them.
ten.when: Sleeve it against creature pods where you are not the only one going wide; it is the bench's best-ranked card at EDHREC 1026 and the only one that builds a board on other people's turns.

ten.why: Attack, hand a creature deathtouch, and if that creature connects the Sanguinist becomes prepared — letting you cast a copy of Exsanguinate, which drains each opponent for X and gains you that much; with Bloodletter of Aclazotz out on your turn each opponent loses 2X instead.
ten.when: Sleeve it for grindy tables where the alpha strike gets chumped: it converts a single connection into a repeatable X-spell finisher, and the lifegain half is more loop ignition on top.

ten.why: Interaction-breadth answers 4 of 5 permanent classes and graveyard is the one uncovered; 'exile target player's graveyard' is the cheapest answer on the bench that is never a dead card, because the other two modes are a Pest token or a draw.
ten.when: Sleeve it for any pod with a reanimator or a graveyard-value deck. It beat Cemetery Gatekeeper for the graveyard slot: the Gatekeeper's damage is symmetric and taxes your own land drops, while the Bloodmage is a Vampire, so casting it also banks an eminence token.

bench_verdicts.why: The obsolescence index lists Bloodline Keeper // Lord of Lineage as strictly better, and that card is already in the 99 — the box copy is behind something sleeved.
Same finding: the index lists Preacher of the Schism among its replacements, and the Preacher is already in the maindeck.

bench_verdicts.card: Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose
bench_verdicts.why: A second copy of a card the 99 already runs — a spare, not a candidate.
Also a duplicate of a maindeck card, and the maindeck copy is itself a natural cut: the Blood-token engine has almost nothing in the 99 that wants Blood tokens.

bench_verdicts.card: Runo Stromkirk // Krothuss, Lord of the Deep
bench_verdicts.why: Blue front face — outside Edgar's Mardu identity and unplayable here.
A clean deathtouch-lifelink wall at {B}{B}, but Blood Artist takes the cheap-Vampire slot: same cost, an engine instead of a body.
The Aetherborn's job for one more mana, and both lost the slot to Blood Artist.

buff:attached is a real role gap and +2/+2 per death on a Vampire is a fast clock — but it needs a carrier and a combat step, and Mirkwood Bats monetizes the same deaths and the tokens without either.

bench_verdicts.card: Sorin of House Markov // Sorin, Ravenous Neonate
bench_verdicts.why: A two-mana lifelink extort body that flips on any 3-life turn; genuinely close, and the first card back if the extort drain matters more than the draw two Scheming Silvertongue offers.
It fetches a Vampire to the TOP of the library, not to hand — a turn of delay on a soft tutor, and the halves it can reach are Vito and Bloodthirsty Conqueror only, never the enchantments.
Answers the graveyard class, but its 2 damage triggers on every player including you, and the deck's plan is gaining life, not paying it.
A fourth lord behind Legion Lieutenant, Stromkirk Captain and Captivating Vampire; the pump axis is already the deck's deepest.

bench_verdicts.card: Aclazotz, Deepest Betrayal // Temple of the Dead
bench_verdicts.why: A strong five-drop in a curve that peaks at 18 cards each at two and three mana, and its discard plan advances neither the drain nor the tokens.
Seven mana for evasion the alpha strike would love, in a deck whose measured kills do not need a combat step.
Blood tokens and a discard payoff in a 99 with neither; its only bench partner is Wedding Security, also off-list.
A Blood-token payoff with no Blood producers in the maindeck.
Same Blood-token package, one token deep — a value creature, not an engine.
Blood tokens gated on connecting for combat damage; the red slots in this deck are already the tightest on sources.
One Blood token on death — a fine body, no engine, and red pips the manabase is 6 sources short on.
Transforms on attacking with exactly two creatures, which is the one board state a go-wide deck tries never to have.
A Human Soldier: no eminence token on cast, no lord pump, no Sanctum Seeker trigger. Flying for the counters crew is not worth being outside the tribe.
A one-mana vigilance body whose only ability costs {4}{W} for one counter.
Grants intimidate to one creature per black creature entering; Cover of Darkness gives the whole tribe fear for the same mana, and even that is a natural cut here.
First strike and counters on combat damage — a combat-only enchantment in the deck's least-supported colour.
Attack-gated draw that eats the same bodies Viscera Seer and Grave Pact want, at combat speed only.
The tokens are Bats, so they miss every lord, Shared Animosity and Sanctum Seeker's attack trigger.
A two-mana flier that cannot block; the 99 already runs 29 creatures and does not need another body.

gaps: Every combo line in the ten is unverified. Marauding Blight-Priest x Exquisite Blood and x Bloodthirsty Conqueror both need a /resolve-stack run before either is stated as fact.

Mirkwood Bats needs its own scenario for a different reason: whether four simultaneously created tokens are four triggers or one is the entry-counting question stack 008 settled for Purphoros, and nothing here settles it for the Bats. The floor is one drain per creation event plus one per Viscera Seer sacrifice.

cards.csv carries no oracle text for Scheming Silvertongue // Sign in Blood or Stensian Sanguinist // Exsanguinate, so card_roles files both as bare threat:body, the synergy graph has no entry for the Sanguinist at all, and the obsolescence index cannot see either. Both were read off the Scryfall dump's card faces; their ranking rests on oracle text alone.

No pick carries a synergy claim. The synergy graph's shortlist for all ten contains no card in this deck, and the pool brief's 25 synergy candidates are every one of them an 'Aura + Protection' edge hanging off Swiftfoot Boots and Teferi's Protection — a format-wide shortlist finding the deck's protection spells, not its engines.

colour-sources is the one measured deficit the ten does not touch: black is 11 sources short of the Karsten target and 16 lands enter tapped against a target of 8. That is a manabase swap, not a Short List slot, and no bench card is a land.

Ramp closes once, not fully: it measures 7 against a 10-12 target and only Master of Dark Rites answers it from the bench. The remaining 2-4 copies would have to come from the pool as rocks, which no evidence channel here surfaced.

The deck's cards.json carries no edhrec_rank for sideboard entries, so the fact brief reports every bench card as unranked; the ranks quoted above come from cards.csv, the same source the pool brief uses.
